- Use the imperative mood, e.g. `Add README.md`, not `Added README.md`.
- Capitalize the first letter of the subject.
- Do not end the subject with a period.
- A scope or category prefix may be used when useful, e.g.
- Non-trivial commits should include a body.
- Separate the subject and body with a blank line.
- Explain what changed and why. Do not repeat implementation details that are
- Prefer present tense for the current situation and imperative mood for the
- Use paragraphs or bullet lists when they improve clarity.
- Split the work into smaller commits if the body becomes too long.
- Use meaningful branch names in kebab-case, e.g. `refactor-ui-tests`.
description: Apply the SE-EDU Java coding standard for this project when creating, editing, reviewing, or formatting Java code.
Use this skill for every Java code change in this project.
Follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard, basic + intermediate rules. For topics
not covered by the SE-EDU standard, fall back to the Google Java Style Guide.
- Package names must be all lower case.
- The root package should be the project name, followed by logical package
- Class and enum names must be nouns in PascalCase.
- Variable names must be in camelCase.
- Method names must be verbs in camelCase.
- Constant names must be in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE.
- Boolean variables and boolean methods should read like booleans, preferably
- Collection names should usually be plural.
- Use 4 spaces for indentation. Do not use tabs.
- Keep lines under 120 characters. Prefer wrapping before 110 characters when
- Wrapped lines should normally be indented by 8 spaces from the parent line.
- Separate logical units within a block with blank lines.
- Every class must be in a package.
- Imports must be explicit. Do not use wildcard imports.
static imports, blank line, `java`/`javax` imports, blank line, third-party
- Attach array specifiers to the type, e.g. `String[] args`.
- Declare variables in the smallest possible scope and initialize them where
- Do not use public variables except constants or simple data-only classes.
- Use braces for all `if`, `else`, `for`, `while`, and `do-while` bodies.
- Put conditionals on their own line.
- In `switch` statements, include an explicit `// Fallthrough` comment when a
- Comments must be in English, use American spelling, and avoid local slang.
- Write descriptive header comments for all public classes and public methods,
except simple getters/setters, inherited overrides whose parent Javadoc
- Use standard Javadoc format with a short first-sentence summary.
- In method Javadocs, start summaries with forms such as `Returns ...`,
- When using `@param`, `@return`, or `@throws`, include all relevant entries and
- Indent comments according to the surrounding code.
- Run `./gradlew javadoc` when Javadocs were added or changed.

description: Run project UI tests for this Java chatbot from test/ui-test-plan.md, comparing command lists against expected console output and stopping immediately on the first mismatch.
Use this skill when asked to run, add, review, or update UI tests for this project.
Each test case may also include:
- initial contents of a file before the program starts
- expected contents of a file after the program exits
- runs `java -cp /tmp/cs2103-ip-ui-tests computah.Duke` once per test case
- optionally creates files recorded as `Initial file `path/to/file.txt`:`
- sends the listed inputs through standard input
- compares actual output against expected output after normalizing line endings and trimming trailing whitespace on each line
- optionally compares files recorded as `Expected file `path/to/file.txt`:`
- prints a console input/output record for each completed test
- stops immediately on the first failed test and prints actual versus expected output
If the user provides new commands and expected outputs, update `test/ui-test-plan.md` first, then run the script.

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* IDE and level of expertise: Amateur
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.
Follow the project-specific `seedu-java-coding-standard` skill for all Java code in this project. Apply it when creating, editing, reviewing, or formatting Java source and test code.
Follow the project-specific `seedu-git-standard` skill for all future branches, commits, and commit messages in this project.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.
After each code update, check whether `test/ui-test-plan.md` needs to be updated to cover the changed behavior. If it does, update the test plan before running tests.

After each code update, invoke the project-specific `test-ui` skill to run the UI tests recorded in `test/ui-test-plan.md`. Report the console input/output record from the test session, and if a test fails, stop immediately and report the expected and actual outputs.
Maintain JUnit coverage for the top ~50% highest-value methods, prioritizing complex, core, or critical business logic over trivial getters/setters and simple wiring code.

After each code update, check whether existing JUnit tests need to be updated or new JUnit tests need to be added to keep that 50% high-value coverage target. Run the Gradle JUnit test suite after code changes, in addition to the UI test suite.
